Cambridge's structure for a MASTER'S personal statement, from the one university booklet found that treats it as its own genre rather than as a cover letter. "Statements for postgraduate study vary widely from course to course, university to university, country to country. You need a different statement for each postgraduate application." Introduction (what you are applying for, the headlines of your argument, and the structure to follow), a discussion answering six questions -- (1) why this specific course at this specific university, (2) how the course fits your skill set, (3) what makes you stand out from other applicants (work experience, societies, published or presented papers, awards), (4) who or what your main academic influences have been and why, (5) how the course fits your career plans, (6) what else you can contribute to the department -- then a conclusion restating why this course at this university. Writing rules, verbatim: "Use short sentences: 25-30 words is a rough maximum"; "Treat academic and scientific jargon with caution. Not all readers will be admissions tutors, and not all admissions tutors will be experts on your subject"; "It's OK to use headings"; "Use a factual, causal sentence structure: statement + evidence". And the test to draft against: "Imagine that you have to win over a sceptic who thinks that you're applying to do a Masters simply as an excuse to stay at university for a little longer and to put off choosing a career." Also: "A personal statement should 'feel' academic, i.e. a factual document with an introduction, a well-structured discussion backed up by evidence, and a clear conclusion." And what the tutor is reading for beyond the subject: "critical analysis, independent thinking, time and information management, written communication", plus "why you think that postgraduate study is the right career decision for you".
Source (tier): University of Cambridge Careers Service, 'CVs & Applications for Undergraduate & Masters Students' (2017, 43pp)

Rule: THREE NAMED FAILURE MODES for a master's statement, each with Cambridge's own example, and they are the three a language model produces by default. (1) CLICHES: "'I have always wanted to study [subject]' or 'My passion for [subject] goes all the way back to my childhood...'". (2) IMPERSONAL STATEMENTS ABOUT THE SUBJECT: "'Climate change is the most pressing issue for contemporary society' or 'History is key to understanding the big questions of the present'". (3) GENERIC PHRASES ABOUT THE UNIVERSITY: "'I was inspired by [the course's] world-famous teaching staff and the first-rate facilities available' or 'The reputation of [the university] for cutting-edge scientific advances is my chief motivation for applying'". The same booklet's application-writing pages generalise it -- "Demonstrate, don't commentate", "If an adjective or adverb can be cut out, always cut it out. Give facts, not opinions", "Prefer the active to the passive", "Resist the urge to sound clever" -- and rule out the self-assessment sentence by name: "'X and Y make me the ideal candidate for this position' -- personal opinion, and quite an arrogant one! The employer decides who their ideal candidate is"; "'I have excellent communication skills' -- proof is needed"; "'I am passionate about international development' -- passion is good, but you can't just say it. What have you actually done with your passion?". On a CHANGE OF DIRECTION, which is S-029's applicant: explain the transition "as far as possible, showing it as a logical evolution" by answering what skills or knowledge from the previous study help here, why you are changing field, and how the transition fits your career plans. STAR is given as the story structure, with Situation kept shortest, Action longest and Result compulsory, an optional second R for Reflection where the destination asks you to learn from mistakes, and one caution worth keeping: "Aim for a good balance -- make sure they're not all academic examples."
